text: Reading a checklist is one thing; filling out a real write-up with it is another. This lab walks through a complete, honest benchmarking document for Grover's algorithm at N equals 8, section by section, using only numbers already verified earlier in this course.

Every honest write-up has six sections: problem statement, classical baseline, quantum approach, experimental or verified numbers, honest caveats, and bottom-line verdict. Name the real problem, then the best honest classical strategy, then the actual quantum circuit and its real computed numbers, then every caveat that narrows the claim, and only then a verdict.

Filled in for Grover at N equals 8: the classical baseline is 8 worst case, 4.5 average. The quantum approach computes t star as floor of pi over 4 times root 8, which is 2. The verified number is P of marked at iteration 2, exactly 0.9453, the peak. The caveats include that oracle cost isn't included in the iteration count, that this needs genuinely unstructured search, and that the number assumes a noiseless circuit. Nothing here is invented — every entry reuses a number already verified in Chapter 4.

Notice what this structure prevents: you cannot honestly write the bottom-line verdict without the classical baseline and the caveats already in place. That forced completeness is exactly the discipline casual claims about quantum advantage tend to skip. The same six sections work for any algorithm in this course — Shor's against the General Number Field Sieve, or Simon's against its proven 2 to the n over 2 lower bound.
Next lesson is the capstone: pick one algorithm from this course and do everything it has modeled lesson by lesson — derive it, verify it, and benchmark it honestly, once, end to end.
